title: Field Notes
text:
A decade in the wild · 2007—2016



Thousands of monthly visits to 60 US national parks, set beside the temperatures and precipitation that shape a day outside. Explore the broad pattern, then step inside one park at a time.


7,176park-month observations


54national parks


2007–2016years covered

title: Field Notes
text:
The national picture
Each point is one park-month. The warm band is busy: visitation rises as outdoor conditions become more comfortable, but the relationship is not a straight line. Desert parks often trade summer heat for winter crowds, while high-latitude parks compress their season into a few bright months.


Code
overview <- parks |>
  mutate(year = factor(year))

plot_ly(
  overview,
  x = ~average_temperature_f,
  y = ~visitor_count,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~year,
  colors = "YlOrRd",
  size = ~precipitation_in,
  sizes = c(6, 28),
  opacity = .55,
  text = ~paste(park_name, month_name, year, sep = " · "),
  hovertemplate = "%{text}<br>%{x:.0f}°F · %{y:,.0f} visits<extra></extra>"
) |>
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Average monthly temperature (°F)", zeroline = FALSE),
    yaxis = list(title = "Monthly visitor count", tickformat = ","),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Year"))
  )

title: Field Notes
text:
Start exploring
Use the Exploration tab to select an individual park, zoom into a time period, and compare its visitor curve with local temperature and precipitation. The Story follows one focused question: why do northern and desert parks peak in opposite seasons?

Data note: annual visitation totals come from the National Park Service Stats archive via TidyTuesday. Monthly counts and weather values are a reproducible teaching approximation derived from annual totals and regional climate profiles; see the data-preparation script for the method.

title: Exploration
text:
Interactive data tool



The dropdown changes the visible traces; the built-in range slider lets you focus on a particular stretch of the decade. Hover over a line to inspect individual months.

title: Exploration
text:
Visitors over time


Code
visitor_buttons <- map(park_names, function(park) {
  list(method = "update", args = list(list(visible = park_names == park), list(title = park)), label = park)
})

visitor_plot <- plot_ly()
for (park in park_names) {
  current <- filter(parks, park_name == park)
  visitor_plot <- add_trace(visitor_plot, data = current, x = ~date, y = ~visitor_count,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = park, visible = park == default_park,
    line = list(color = "#d6674d", width = 2.5),
    hovertemplate = "%{x|%b %Y}<br>%{y:,.0f} visitors<extra></extra>")
}
visitor_plot |>
  layout(
    title = list(text = default_park),
    xaxis = list(title = NULL, rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)),
    yaxis = list(title = "Monthly visitors", tickformat = ","),
    updatemenus = list(list(type = "dropdown", active = which(park_names == default_park) - 1, buttons = visitor_buttons, x = 0, y = 1.16, xanchor = "left")),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )








Figure 1

title: Exploration
text:
Weather alongside the crowds


Code
weather_buttons <- map(park_names, function(park) {
  visible <- rep(FALSE, length(park_names) * 2)
  visible[(match(park, park_names) * 2) - 1:0] <- TRUE
  list(method = "update", args = list(list(visible = visible), list(title = park)), label = park)
})

weather_plot <- plot_ly()
for (park in park_names) {
  current <- filter(parks, park_name == park)
  weather_plot <- add_trace(weather_plot, data = current, x = ~date, y = ~average_temperature_f,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Temperature", visible = park == default_park,
    line = list(color = "#e7a24b", width = 2.5), hovertemplate = "%{x|%b %Y}<br>%{y:.0f}°F<extra></extra>")
  weather_plot <- add_trace(weather_plot, data = current, x = ~date, y = ~precipitation_in,
    type = "bar", name = "Precipitation", visible = park == default_park,
    marker = list(color = "#8da99a"), hovertemplate = "%{x|%b %Y}<br>%{y:.1f} in<extra></extra>")
}
weather_plot |>
  layout(
    title = list(text = default_park),
    xaxis = list(title = NULL, rangeslider = list(visible = TRUE)),
    yaxis = list(title = "Temperature (°F) / precipitation (in)"),
    barmode = "overlay",
    updatemenus = list(list(type = "dropdown", active = which(park_names == default_park) - 1, buttons = weather_buttons, x = 0, y = 1.16, xanchor = "left")),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)
  )








Figure 2





The park selector is embedded in each chart so it works on a static site without a Shiny server.

title: Story
text:
A seasonal field note



There is no single national park season. In the north, winter closes the door and summer opens it. In the desert, summer heat does the opposite: the comfortable months arrive after the crowds have gone.

title: Story
text:
01 / Summer is not one thing


Code
story_parks <- c("Glacier", "Acadia", "Death Valley", "Zion")
seasonal <- parks |>
  filter(park_name %in% story_parks) |>
  mutate(season = if_else(month %in% 6:8, "Summer", "Winter")) |>
  group_by(park_name, season) |>
  summarise(visitors = sum(visitor_count), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(park_name = forcats::fct_reorder(park_name, visitors, .fun = sum))

ggplot(seasonal, aes(park_name, visitors, fill = season)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = .7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Summer" = "#d6674d", "Winter" = "#8da99a")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Visitors (millions)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Manrope") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")








Figure 1: Estimated summer and winter visitor totals for two northern and two desert parks.





Glacier and Acadia concentrate their welcome into warm months. Zion and Death Valley spread their opportunity differently: heat changes the timing of a visit, rather than erasing demand altogether. A national average would flatten this useful contrast.

title: Story
text:
02 / Peaks are weather-shaped


Code
events <- parks |>
  filter(park_name %in% c("Glacier", "Death Valley")) |>
  group_by(park_name, month_name, month) |>
  summarise(visitors = sum(visitor_count), temperature = mean(average_temperature_f), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(events, aes(month, visitors, color = park_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Glacier" = "#d6674d", "Death Valley" = "#e7a24b")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly visitors (millions)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Manrope") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")








Figure 2: Visitor counts and temperature profiles for Glacier and Death Valley.





The curves are mirror images because the operational seasons are mirror images. Snowpack, road access, heat exposure, and daylight all turn a temperature reading into a practical decision: when can visitors arrive, move through the landscape, and stay comfortable long enough to explore?

title: Story
section: A picture of the shoulder season
text:
A picture of the shoulder season





A mountain landscape in a cool-season light.






A warm desert landscape under open sky.





Interpretation: these visuals use modeled monthly weather profiles, not event-level NOAA observations. They are best read as a clear demonstration of the seasonal mechanism, not as a causal estimate of weather’s independent effect.
